Please accept the attached comments on U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Proposed Rule entitled Federal 
Implementation Plans Under the Clean Air Act for Indian Reservations in Idaho, Oregon, and Washington and 
revisions to the Federal Air Rules for Reservations (FARR), which were published in the Federal Register on October 
12, 2022, 87 Fed. Reg. 61870. 
PotlatchDeltic Corporation (PotlatchDeltic) operates a highly regulated wood products facility in St. Maries, Idaho 
on the Coeur d'Alene Reservation, known as the St. Maries Complex (SMC). The Proposed Rule will increase the 
already significant regulatory burden on PotlatchDeltic by expanding applicability of the PMio emissions limitations 
in 40 CFR § 49.128 to the veneer dryers at the SMC. The justification expressed by EPA the for the proposal is not 
supported by information readily available to the public or in the formal rulemaking docket. In addition, the 
proposed revisions to 40 CFR § 49.126 may result in costly and impractical requirements for control of fugitive dust 
emissions without valuable input from facilities. 
PotlatchDeltic requests reconsideration and deletion of these revisions for the Coeur d'Alene Reservation and the 
St. Maries Complex.

PotlatchDeltic Corporation's Comments regarding the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Proposed Rule to 
revise the Federal Air Rules for Reservations ("FARR")  
Docket No. EPA-R1O-OAR-2020-0361 
Relevant Proposed FARR Revisions. 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency ("EPA") proposes to apply 40 CFR § 49.128, which limits PMio emissions 
from wood products industry sources, to the Coeur d'Alene Reservation because the operations of PotlatchDeltic 
Corporation's ("PotlatchDeltic") St. Maries Complex ("SMC") may contribute to the elevated levels of particulate 
matter or PM2.5. 87 Fed. Reg. 61870, 61878, 61885 (Oct. 12, 2022) (proposing to amend 40 CFR §§ 49.128, 
49.9926(e), and 49.9930(e)); Supporting Statement at 20, Dkt. No. EPA-R1O-OAR-2020-0361-0078. 
EPA proposes to authorize EPA Region 10 ("R10") to revise a facility's fugitive dust plan, if EPA R10 unilaterally 
determines that the plan is not adequate to prevent or minimize emissions. See 87 Fed. Reg. 61896-97 (proposing 
to amend 40 CFR § 49.126(d)(2)). 
Relevant SMC Background 
The SMC is located along the St. Joe River near the intersection of Railroad Avenue and Mill Road in northwest St. 
Maries, Idaho. The facility is within the Coeur d'Alene Reservation and is in Indian Country as defined in 40 CFR 
Part 71. The SMC consists of a sawmill, lumber dry kilns, planer mill, and plywood mill. The plywood mill produces 
plywood using various equipment, including four steam-heated veneer dryers. Emissions from the heating zones 
of the veneer dryers are captured and controlled by a regenerative catalytic oxidizer ("RCO") to comply with 40 
CFR Part 63, Subpart DDDD. See, Minor New Source Review Permit No. R1OTNSR01800 Permit Analysis. 
Compliance with this federal standard results in effective co-benefit reductions of volatile organic compounds 
("y0C") and particulate matter ("PM") emissions. RCO source test data confirms compliance with the FARR PM 
limit.1 
The SMC is regulated by: 
•
a minor new source review permit issued by EPA in 2021, Permit No. R1OTNSR01803, available at 
https://www.epa.govicaa-permitting/potlatchdeltic-land-and-lumber-11c-tribal-nninor-new-source-review-
nsr-air-permit; 
1  Source test data provided to EPA shows PM emissions from the veneer dryers at 0.028 pounds per thousand 
square feet (lb/msf) on a 3/8" basis. The measured PM emissions are less than 9 percent of the PM10 emission 
limit (0.3 lb/msf, 3/8" basis) established by 40 CFR § 49.128.

federal emissions limitations under 40 CFR Part 63, Subpart DDDD;

the FARR; and

06/documents/190621 potlatchdeltic mnsr analysis.pdf 
EPA's Justification for the FARR Revisions Impacting the SMC and PotlatchDeltic Comments.  
1) 
EPA R10 justifies the proposed FARR revisions and specifically the extension of 40 CFR § 49.128 to the 
Coeur d'Alene Reservation as necessary and appropriate based on the input, coordination, and 
consultation with affected Tribes. According to the preamble, EPA R10 actively coordinated and consulted 
with affected Tribes in both group and individual meetings and encouraged affected Tribes to provide 
input to the EPA R10 in developing these proposed revisions to ensure that Tribal considerations are 
properly addressed. EPA R10 describes their coordination and consultation with affected Tribes in the 
docket for this action. 87 Fed. Reg. 61871; see also Federal Air Rules for Reservations Revisions 
Coordination and Consultation Record ("Consultation Record") (Sept. 2022), Dkt. No. EPA-R1O-OAR-2020-
0361-075. According to the preamble, EPA R10 revised the FARR to apply on specific Indian reservations 
where the EPA finds, in coordination and consultation with the relevant Tribes, that the rules are 
necessary or appropriate. 87 Fed. Reg. 61885. 
PotlatchDeltic Comment: The rulemaking docket reveals that the consultation and coordination with the 
Coeur d'Alene Tribe did not include discussion of the SMC, the impacts of PM emissions from the SMC, nor 
any discussion of the need or benefits of expanding 40 CFR § 49.128 to cover the SMC. According to the 
docket, consultation and coordination with the Coeur d'Alene Tribe was limited to one 2020 webinar 
presented to "All Tribes" and a 2021 phone call regarding residential wood stoves. 
EPA R10 proposed the change to 40 CFR § 49.128 unilaterally. See, Memorandum from Sandra Brozusky, 
Tribal Air Team Lead, Re: Basis for the Applicability of the Additional FARR Rules to Specific Indian 
Reservations ("Brozusky Mem.") (Sept. 8, 2022), Dkt. No. EPA-R10-0AR-2020-0361-0053; Consultation 
Record, Dkt. No. EPA-R10-0AR-2020-0361-075. 
3 

Based on information readily available to the public or in the formal rulemaking docket the proposed 
revision of 40 CFR § 49.128 to apply to the veneer dryers at the SMC is unsupported by input from the 
Coeur d'Alene Tribe. 
Notably, EPA R10 did not coordinate with the regulated community impacted by this revision nor initiate a 
negotiated rulemaking process. See, Consultation Record, Dkt. No. EPA-R10-0AR-2020-0361-075. 
2) 
According to the preamble, EPA R10 does not intend, nor does it expect the proposed revisions to impose 
significantly different regulatory burdens upon industry or residents within reservations than those 
imposed by the rules of state and local air agencies in the surrounding areas. Instead, the intent remains 
to ensure that people living within reservation boundaries receive equivalent air quality protection, and 
that emissions from sources located within reservations are controlled to levels similar to those of sources 
located outside the Indian reservations. 87 Fed. Reg 61872 (proposing to amend 40 CFR §§ 49.128, 
49.9926(e), and 49.9930(e)). 
EPA R10 repeats throughout the preamble, that a key goal of the FARR was "to 'level the playing field" 
and help ensure that emissions from sources located within reservations are controlled to levels similar to 
those of sources located outside the Indian reservations. 87 Fed. Reg. 61872 (proposing to amend 40 CFR 
§§ 49.128, 49.9926(e), and 49.9930(e)) 
Further EPA R10's justification observes that the Coeur d'Alene Reservation encompasses a portion of the 
City of St. Maries and includes the SMC. EPA R10 proposes to apply 40 CFR § 49.128 to this reservation. In 
2005, EPA R10 applied this rule to the Colville and Nez Perce Reservations because there were wood 
product facilities operating on those reservations. EPA R10 states that the SMC is in the same source 
category and applying this rule to the Coeur d'Alene Reservation would level the playing field with these 
similar emission sources and bring applicable emission standards for the SMC more in line with those 
applicable to similar sources in Idaho. Brozusky Mem., Dkt. No. EPA-R1O-OAR-2020-0361-0053. 
PotlatchDeltic Comment: People living on the Coeur d'Alene Reservation receive robust air quality 
protection from the layers of EPA R10 regulation and permitting already imposed on the SMC. The SMC is 
more strictly regulated than similar sources in Idaho and wood products operators located on other 
reservations in Region 10. See, e.g., Stimson Lumber, St. Maries permit issued by Idaho DEQ dated 
November 14, 2022, httas://www2.deq.idaho.qov/admin/LEIA/index.html?view=folder&id=3251. 
4 

The proposal to expand 40 CFR § 49.128 to the SMC is unnecessary to "level the playing field" because the 
SMC is already subject to effective emissions limitations that exceed the regulatory burden of similar 
sources located on and off Indian reservations. As previously described, PM emissions from the SMC are 
strictly limited by EPA R10 permits. These permits combined with applicable federal standards exceed the 
level of PM emissions control imposed on similar sources located off the Reservation. Expanding 40 CFR § 
49.128 to the SMC adds a layer of redundant regulatory burden without enhancing air quality protections 
for residents on or off the Reservation. 
3)
According to EPA's statements, the extension of 40 CFR § 49.128 to the Coeur d'Alene Reservation and 
the SMC is not expected to result in new capital costs for PotlatchDeltic. This is because EPA R10 
concludes that the emission controls that the facility is currently using to comply with 40 CFR Part 63, 
Subpart DDDD (the regenerative catalytic oxidizer) will control PM emissions to below the levels required 
in 40 CFR § 49.128. 87 Fed. Reg. 61887. 
PotlatchDeltic Comment: As noted by EPA R10, the SMC is subject to federal regulations, including 40 CFR 
Part 63, Subpart DDDD, which requires VOC emissions controls that also reduce PM emissions to below the 
FARR requirement. Even if the proposal does not require additional capital costs, the proposal will result in 
increased costs for the SMC. The expanded FARR regulations, as proposed, do not include source testing, 
monitoring, or requirements; however, 40 CFR § 49.123(b) and (c) allow for EPA R10 to require gap-filling 
provisions for source testing, monitoring, and recordkeeping as part of the permitting process. The SMC is 
subject to air permit requirements in 40 CFR Part 71, and EPA R10 will likely include gap-filling provisions 
into the SMC operating permit. New testing, monitoring, or recordkeeping under the expanded 40 CFR § 
49.128 will result in additional costs to comply with the FARR. Extending the FARR to the SMC, which is 
already subject to stringent emissions controls, is a redundant layering of requirements. The proposed 
revisions will increase the burden to demonstrate compliance with both the FARR and MACT obligations, 
along with existing rigorous and unique EPA R10 permitting obligations, resulting in layers of requirements 
that are not imposed on similar sources. The proposal creates duplication of regulatory requirements and 
will result in increased costs, without any additional environmental protection or benefit. 
4)
EPA R10 observes that 40 CFR § 49.128 will continue to apply on the Colville Reservation and the Nez 
Perce Reservation. EPA R10 proposes that 40 CFR § 49.128 be applied on the Coeur d'Alene Reservation 
because the operations of a wood products facility located on the Coeur d'Alene Reservation may 
contribute to elevated levels of PM. 87 Fed. Reg. 61878; see also Economic Analysis, § A.5.2, Dkt. No. EPA-
R1O-OAR-2020-0361-0023. 
PotlatchDeltic Comment: While the language of 40 CFR § 49.128 applies to the Colville and Nez Perce 
Reservations (See, 40 CFR §§ 49.9956(f), 49.9960(f); 40 CFR §§ 49 10406(f), 49.10410(f)), there are no 
5 

emissions sources or wood products facilities like the SMC on these reservations. No sources on these 
reservations are subject to the emissions limitation in 40 CFR § 49.128 (See, Dkt. No. EPA-R1O-OAR-2020-
0361-0012). 
•
The wood products facility on the Coville Reservation (Omak Forest Products) closed in 2017. 
•
The wood products facility on the Nez Perce Reservation (Clearwater Forest Industries, Inc.) does not 
operate high temperature veneer dryers, is not subject to the stringent federal standards at 40 CFR 
Part 63, Subpart DDDD, nor subject to stringent operational and emissions limits like those in EPA R10 
permits issued to PotlatchDeltic. See, Non-Title V Air Quality Operating Permit No. R1ONT500701. This 
permit does not include 40 CFR § 49.128 as an applicable requirement. 
•
The only other wood products facility on the Nez Perce Reservation (Empire Lumber Company dba 
Kamiah Mills) does not operate high temperature veneer dryers, is not subject to the federal 
standards at 40 CFR Part 63, Subpart DDDD, nor subject to stringent operational and emissions limits 
like those in EPA R10 permits issued to PotlatchDeltic. See, Non-Title V Air Quality Operating Permit 
No. R1OTNSR03000. This permit does not include 40 CFR § 49.128 as an applicable requirement. 
5) 
EPA R10 states that expanding 40 CFR § 49.128 to the Coeur d'Alene Reservation is necessary because 
operations at the SMC may contribute to elevated levels of PM2.5 in St. Maries, Idaho. 87 Fed. Reg. 
61885. 
PotlatchDeltic Comment: The evaluation of PM2.5 emissions as a basis for expansion of 40 CFR § 49.128 
to the Coeur d'Alene Reservation is flawed. 
•
First, 40 CFR § 49.128 limits PM10 emissions, not PM2.5 emissions. This section of the FARR does not 
regulate PM2.5 emissions. 
•
Second, PM emissions from the SMC veneer dryers are already controlled by a state-of-the art RCO. 
Based on information readily available to the public or in the formal rulemaking docket, no other 
plywood mill in Region 10 located on tribal land within EPA jurisdiction operates this level of PM 
control on veneer dryers. EPA R10 recognizes that measured emissions from the SMC veneer dryers 
are well below the FARR limit in 40 CFR § 49.128. Therefore, imposing the limit established in 40 CFR § 
49.128 on the SMC will not provide additional air quality protection nor reduce emissions that are 
already well below the FARR limit, nor level the playing field. The proposal only adds unnecessary 
burden and cost to PotlatchDeltic. 
•
Third, to address PM2.5 emissions in the St. Maries, Idaho airshed PotlatchDeltic is working with the 
St. Maries Airshed PM Advance Program (PM Advance Program) 
(https://www.epa.aov/systemniles/documents/2021-09/id-st-maries-2021-path-forward-.pda Data 
prepared under the PM Advance Program indicates the SMC is only the fourth largest anthropogenic 
source of PM2.5 emissions in the airshed after a different wood products facility (not located on the 
Reservation), residential wood combustion, and paved roadways. Speciation of PM2.5 filters collected 
in the airshed along with source apportionment modeling confirm that the SMC veneer dryers do not 
contribute materially to elevated PM2.5 concentrations. PotlatchDeltic also partners with other 
stakeholders to fund targeted woodstove change-outs, tackling one of the top three sources of PM2.5 
emissions in the airshed. 
6 

6) 
The existing FARR requires facilities to develop a fugitive dust plan, implement reasonable precautions to 
prevent fugitive dust, and provides eight examples of reasonable precautions, 40 CFR § 49.126(d)(2). The 
proposal authorizes EPA R10 to revise a facility's fugitive dust plan unilaterally, if EPA R10 determines that 
the plan is inadequate to prevent or minimize emissions. 
PotlatchDeltic Comment: The proposal could allow EPA R10 to require fugitive dust control measures that 
are not reasonable or achievable for a specific operation without any process for the facility to respond to 
a unilateral determination or to new requirements. This approach establishes a subjective test where 
multiple people, even within EPA R10, could have different interpretations of what is reasonable without 
input from the facility. EPA R10 estimates no additional costs to implement the revisions to 40 CFR § 
49.126; however, there will certainly be additional capital and operating costs to implement additional 
fugitive dust control measures that EPA R10 unilaterally requires. 
Conclusion and Requests. 
According to information readily available to the public or in the formal rulemaking docket, the Coeur d'Alene 
Tribe did not provide input on, request, or prompt the expansion of 40 CFR § 49.128. 
According to information readily available to the public or in the formal rulemaking docket, the SMC is the most 
highly regulated wood products facility in Region 10. If EPA R10 were truly seeking to "level the playing field" and 
bring facilities in line with similar sources, then 40 CFR § 49.128 would not apply to the SMC. Instead, more robust 
emissions and operating limitations would be imposed on the facilities located on the Nez Perce Reservation (as 
well as imposing more emissions controls on similar wood products facilities located off reservations in R10) to 
level up to the rigorous regulations that EPA R10 requires of PotlatchDeltic. See  https://www.epa.gov/caa-
permitting/air-permits-issued-epa-region-10. 
According to information readily available to the public or in the formal rulemaking docket, the application of 40 
CFR § 49.128 to the Coeur d'Alene Reservation to align with regulation of similar sources on the Colville and Nez 
Perce Reservations, is an act of form over substance, since no "similar sources" actually exist on the Colville and 
Nez Perce Reservations. 
According to information readily available to the public or in the formal rulemaking docket, EPA failed to consider 
fully the costs of compliance or costs of layered regulatory burdens. EPA failed to evaluate if its proposal to expand 
40 CFR § 49.128 would achieve any actual air quality protection or benefit intended by the proposed rulemaking. 
7

Re: Formal Comments regarding EPA-R10-OAR-2020-0361, Federal Implementation Plans Under the 
Clean Air Act for Indian Reservations in Idaho, Oregon, and Washington 
Dear Tribal Air Team Lead Brozusky, 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on Federal Implementation Plans Under the Clean Air Act for 
Indian Reservations in Idaho, Oregon, and Washington. As the Air Quality Specialist for the Makah Tribe 
(Tribe), I would like to provide comments on the Proposed Revisions to the Federal Air Rules for 
Reservations on behalf of the Tribe. 
Firstly, the Makah Tribe would like to comment on the decision to either relax the threshold for declaring 
burn bans or keep it the same. Previously, a burn ban would be triggered if the 24-hour PM concentrations 
were projected to exceed 75% of the NAAQS. However, it has been proposed to change the threshold to 
whether PM concentrations will exceed or are projected to exceed the NAAQS (rather than 75% of the 
NAAQS) anytime during the next 72 hours. The argument behind this change is that the old threshold 
impeded the use of prescribed fire to prevent wildfires, by limiting the number of available burn days. 
Given the Makah Tribe has been increasingly impacted by wildfire smoke, the proposed change to relax 
the burn ban threshold could be useful in reducing wildfire smoke impacts in the future. Thus, the Tribe 
supports the proposed change to relax the burn ban threshold. 
Secondly, regarding changes to the Residential Woodstove Installation section, there are two options 
provided for the revision. The first option is to only allow future installation of woodstoves certified by 
the EPA in 2015 or newer. The second option is to allow any EPA-certified woodstove to be installed. For 
this revision, the Makah Tribe proposes that EPA should allow the installation of any EPA-certified 
woodstove as long as it meets the 2020 New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) for Residential Wood 
Heaters emission standards. States currently follow this standard so for consistency purposes we 
recommend that tribes be held to the same standard without the added stringency of only allowing 2015 
or newer EPA-certified woodstoves. 
Lastly, Section 49.126 (page 61877), it is unclear if portable rock crushers are required to conduct fugitive 
particulate emission surveys and the announcement, under the rule for this issue (Page 61896) doesn't 
provide any clarity. Therefore, clarity about how changes will affect rock crushing at tribally controlled 
quarries or any of the other quarries used to manufacture rock for forest road applications is needed. 
For any questions, contact me at 360-645-3151 or courtney.winck@makah.com.  

 
Sincerely, 
 
Courtney Winck 
Air Quality Specialist, Makah Tribe

Re: Comments on the Proposal to Revise the Federal Air Rules for Reservations (FARR) 
for Reservations in Idaho, Oregon, and Washington (EPA-R10-OAR-2020-0361).  
 
Dear Sandra Brozusky: 
 
The Northwest Horticultural Council (NHC) and the Washington State Tree Fruit Association 
(WSTFA) are pleased to have the opportunity to comment on the Environmental Protection 
Agency’s (EPA) proposal to revise the Federal Air Rules for Reservations (FARR) under the Clean 
Air Act for Reservations in Idaho, Oregon, and Washington, published in the Federal Register on 
October 12, 2022.  
 
The NHC manages federal and international policy and regulatory issues for growers, packers, and 
shippers of apples, pears, and cherries in Idaho, Oregon, and Washington. Together, our growers 
produce 69 percent of the apples, 88 percent of the pears, and 69 percent of the sweet cherries 
grown in the United States. The WSTFA is a voluntary non-profit association supporting the 
growers, packers, and marketers of apples, pears, cherries, and other deciduous tree fruits in 
Washington with education and training programs, industry statistical information, and 
representation on state and local policy issues. 
 
Frost prevention in tree fruit orchards is crucial early in the growing season, especially during the 
bud and blossom phases. Failure to mitigate cold temperature at these critical times can result in 
tissue death of newly developing fruit buds, resulting in crop loss or even loss of trees. For 
decades growers in the Pacific Northwest have been moving away from diesel-burning heating 
devices (i.e., smudge pots) as a method for maintaining orchard temperatures above certain 
thresholds. In orchards that still have them, smudge pots are used as an emergency measure 
during sustained cold weather events to prevent crop loss. Purchasing, installing, and 
maintaining new, more efficient propane heating devices is expensive and the new technology is 
vulnerable to theft and damage.  
 
As EPA works to revise the FARR regulations regarding orchard heating devices that are subject 
to the 20 percent opacity standard, we request provisions within the new rules that encourage 
transition toward adoption of newer technology and avoid creation of unreasonable burdens on 
tree fruit growers farming on reservations in the Pacific Northwest. These are substantial 

 
2 
 
investments. Orchard establishment can take three to five years and cost between $50,000 and 
$75,000 per acre. 
 
EPA expects that these older methods of orchard heating would not be capable of complying 
with the 20 percent opacity standard and therefore the rules would effectively prohibit the 
continued use of such devices. While newer alternatives such as wind machines and propane 
heaters are being steadily adopted, the purchase costs make it more achievable for large farms or 
vertically integrated operations. The impacts of new visible emissions regulations on smaller, 
family-owned farms must also be considered. EPA should explore ways to incentivize growers to 
install new orchard heating devices. For many growers, the up-front capital costs of replacing 
non-complying devices, and long-term costs of maintaining them, supersede any expected annual 
cost savings from newer, more efficient alternatives. 
 
We appreciate that the proposed 20 percent opacity provision would not go into effect until three 
years after the revision is finalized and the rule becomes effective. Providing this deferred 
implementation is critical for small to medium-sized growers to have time to prepare and plan 
for the installation of new orchard heating methods, as well as to apply for financial assistance, 
potentially via U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) grants.  
 
We strongly support the provision that would allow EPA to grant a two-year renewable 
extension to growers and the absence of a limit on the number of extensions. However, providing 
growers more time to comply may not be enough. Small and medium-sized farms may not have 
the capital or capacity to make the switch to alternative heating devices no matter how many 
extensions are granted. EPA should identify sources of funding that may help lower the costs for 
alternate methods of orchard heating, including through the USDA Natural Resources

necessitate increased cold temperature mitigation, such as the arctic jet stream over central
